metadata.title: Multi-scale Neural Networks for Retinal Blood Vessels Segmentation

extraction_notes.note: Dataset descriptions (DRIVE, STARE, CHASE), training hyper-parameters (Adam, learning rate, hardware), related-work reported numbers and the appendix result tables were not extracted: descriptive or tabulated empirical content without mathematical statements.
Architecture design choices described in prose were typed as algorithm (model specification) rather than definition; AP2 and AP3 are single design moves and have no steps.
Benchmark outcomes were emitted as claims with rigor numerical; only one headline sentence per results subsection was kept, the remaining per-metric comparisons stay unextracted.
Unmarked algorithm steps are sub-sentence operation spans taken from single prose sentences.

metadata.extraction_comment: Applied deep-learning paper with two numbered equations and no theorems; the graph mostly records model components, preprocessing procedures and empirical claims.

nodes.name: Fully convolutional encoder-decoder architecture
nodes.statement: It can be briefly divided into two parts - encoder and decoder. The encoder is a convolutional neural network which extracts features from the input image such as the retinal blood vessels image and the decoder will upsample the extracted features to the result image that we desired, such as the vessels segmentation in our task.
nodes.statement_short: FCN with a convolutional encoder extracting features and a decoder upsampling them to the segmentation map.
input: the input image such as the retinal blood vessels image
output: the result image that we desired, such as the vessels segmentation in our task

nodes.name: Encoder
nodes.statement: The encoder is a convolutional neural network which extracts features from the input image such as the retinal blood vessels image
nodes.statement_short: Extract features with a CNN encoder.

nodes.name: Decoder
nodes.statement: the decoder will upsample the extracted features to the result image that we desired, such as the vessels segmentation in our task
nodes.statement_short: Upsample features to the segmentation image.

nodes.name: Stride-2 convolution replacing pooling
nodes.statement: Pooling layer will cause the missing of some information. Therefore we choose to use convolution operation with stride 2 to replace pooling operation so that the information could be preserved as much as possible and the result feature map has the same size as in pooling layer.
nodes.statement_short: Downsample with stride-2 convolutions instead of pooling to preserve information.

nodes.name: Adjacent-layer feature fusion
nodes.statement: Another modification in the convolutional layer is that we fuse the features extracted from two adjacent convolutional layers together. So that the low-level information could be passed to the top layers and the model could make sufficient use of the effective low-level features to do semantic segmentation.
nodes.statement_short: Fuse features of adjacent convolutional layers so low-level information reaches top layers.

nodes.name: Atrous convolution
nodes.statement: {\bfseries Atrous Convolution} Atrous convolution is an operation that adds "holes" in normal convolutional operation so that the resolution of features could be controlled by these "holes".
differentia: adds "holes" in normal convolutional operation so that the resolution of features could be controlled by these "holes"

nodes.name: Atrous convolution enlarges receptive field with fewer parameters
nodes.statement: Another property of atrous convolution is that it could reduce the parameters in network but expand the reception fields.

nodes.name: Atrous convolution operation
nodes.statement: Suppose there are two-dimensional signals, $x$ is the input feature map and $y$ is the output feature map, $i$ represents each location in $y$ and $W$ is the convolution filter. Then the atrous convolution operation applied on $x$ as follows: \begin{equation} y [ i ] = \sum _ { k } x [ i + r \cdot k ] W [ k ] \end{equation} where $r$ is the rate controls the stride with which the input signal is sampled.
nodes.statement_short: $y[i]=\sum_k x[i+r k]W[k]$ with input $x$, output $y$, filter $W$ and rate $r$.

nodes.name: Atrous convolution formula
nodes.statement: y [ i ] = \sum _ { k } x [ i + r \cdot k ] W [ k ]
nodes.statement_short: Output at $i$ is sum of filter-weighted input samples spaced by rate $r$.

nodes.name: Multi-scale sensitive feature module
nodes.statement: {\bfseries Multi-scale sensitive features} In order to get multi-scale information, we apply 6 atrous convolutional layers with different rate, 1 max pooling layer and 1 average pooling layer simultaneously on the input image, and then concatenate the extracted feature maps to obtain the effective multi-scale feature map, as shown in Figure 1 (2).
nodes.statement_short: Run 6 atrous convolutions with different rates plus max and average pooling in parallel, then concatenate the feature maps.

nodes.name: Parallel atrous and pooling branches
nodes.statement: we apply 6 atrous convolutional layers with different rate, 1 max pooling layer and 1 average pooling layer simultaneously on the input image
nodes.statement_short: Apply 6 atrous convs, max pooling and average pooling in parallel.

nodes.name: Concatenate feature maps
nodes.statement: then concatenate the extracted feature maps to obtain the effective multi-scale feature map
nodes.statement_short: Concatenate branch outputs.

nodes.name: Global Contrast Normalization (GCN)
nodes.statement: For the purpose of better response of neural networks, we perform global contrast normalization that every patch of retinal images is standardized by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of its elements.
differentia: every patch of retinal images is standardized by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of its elements

nodes.name: Automatic Color Enhancement (ACE)
nodes.statement: {\bfseries Automatic Color Enhancement (ACE)} Besides GCN, the automatic color enhancement (ACE), which is a smoothed and localized modification method of the normalized histogram equalization, adjusts the contrast of retinal images to achieve the perceptual constancy of color and brightness.
nodes.genus: a smoothed and localized modification method of the normalized histogram equalization
differentia: adjusts the contrast of retinal images to achieve the perceptual constancy of color and brightness

nodes.name: ACE procedure
nodes.statement: The ACE is divided into three steps. First, we separate the RGB channels of one retinal image $I(x)$ with domain $\Omega$ and scale intensity values to $[0, 1]$. Then, we calculate the $R(x)$ value of each pixel to adapt local image contrast: \begin{equation} R(x) = \sum_{y \in \Omega /\ x}\frac{s_a(I(x) - I(y))}{\left \| x-y \right \|} \ \ \ x \in \Omega \end{equation} where $\Omega /\ x$ denotes $\{y \in \Omega: y \neq x\}$, $\left \| x-y \right \|$ denotes Euclidean distance, and $s_a: [-1,1]\rightarrow R$ is the slope function $s_a(t) = \min \{\max \{ \alpha t, -1 \}, 1\}$ for some $\alpha \geq 1$. For the purpose of the global white balance, we extend $R(x)$ to $[0, 1]$. Finally, we solve the optimization problem.
nodes.statement_short: ACE: scale RGB channels, compute local contrast adaptation $R(x)$ via slope-function weighted differences, stretch to $[0,1]$, then optimize.

nodes.name: Separate channels and scale
nodes.statement: First, we separate the RGB channels of one retinal image $I(x)$ with domain $\Omega$ and scale intensity values to $[0, 1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Split RGB channels, scale to $[0,1]$.

nodes.name: Compute R(x)
nodes.statement: Then, we calculate the $R(x)$ value of each pixel to adapt local image contrast: \begin{equation} R(x) = \sum_{y \in \Omega /\ x}\frac{s_a(I(x) - I(y))}{\left \| x-y \right \|} \ \ \ x \in \Omega \end{equation} where $\Omega /\ x$ denotes $\{y \in \Omega: y \neq x\}$, $\left \| x-y \right \|$ denotes Euclidean distance, and $s_a: [-1,1]\rightarrow R$ is the slope function $s_a(t) = \min \{\max \{ \alpha t, -1 \}, 1\}$ for some $\alpha \geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute local contrast adaptation $R(x)$ with slope function $s_a$.

nodes.name: Extend R(x)
nodes.statement: For the purpose of the global white balance, we extend $R(x)$ to $[0, 1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Stretch $R(x)$ to $[0,1]$ for white balance.

nodes.name: Solve optimization
nodes.statement: Finally, we solve the optimization problem.

nodes.name: ACE local contrast adaptation R(x)
nodes.statement: R(x) = \sum_{y \in \Omega /\ x}\frac{s_a(I(x) - I(y))}{\left \| x-y \right \|} \ \ \ x \in \Omega
nodes.statement_short: $R(x)$ sums slope-function differences $s_a(I(x)-I(y))$ weighted by inverse distance.

nodes.name: Complexity of ACE
nodes.statement: For one retinal image, the complexity of the ACE is $O(N^4)$ and it is too slow to handle all retinal images.

nodes.name: Improved ACE (Getreuer)
nodes.statement: Therefore, we use an improved ACE algorithm proposed by Pascal Getreuer [13]. The new algorithm adopts two approximate methods that they both significantly improve the speed of ACE. One uses polynomial function to approximate the slope function to reduce the calculation and the other uses different degrees of interpolation.
nodes.statement_short: Fast ACE approximating the slope function by a polynomial and using interpolation.

nodes.name: Polynomial slope approximation
nodes.statement: One uses polynomial function to approximate the slope function to reduce the calculation

nodes.name: Interpolation
nodes.statement: the other uses different degrees of interpolation.

nodes.name: Patch-based augmentation
nodes.statement: To overcome this limitation, we use augmentations to increase the number of retinal images to make our model have a good generalization and prevent overfitting. First, the decision of random cropping on the class of a particular 64 $\times$ 64 pixel is based on a patch centered at that pixel of retinal images. For example, we can get a 64 $\times$ 64 $\times$ 3 vector for each patch of retinal images. It should be pointed out that we extract patches after preprocess methods because of the consideration of training and test speed. To further explore augmentations, each patch of retinal images is composed of limited four randomized actions as follows: a) Flipping horizontally or vertically; b) Gamma correction of Saturation and Value (of the HSV colorspace) by raising pixels to a power in [0.25, 4]; c) Rotation by an angle in [-90, 90]; d) Scaling by a factor between 0.7 and 1.3.
nodes.statement_short: Extract 64x64 patches after preprocessing and apply random flips, gamma correction, rotation and scaling.

nodes.name: Random patch cropping
nodes.statement: First, the decision of random cropping on the class of a particular 64 $\times$ 64 pixel is based on a patch centered at that pixel of retinal images. For example, we can get a 64 $\times$ 64 $\times$ 3 vector for each patch of retinal images.
nodes.statement_short: Crop 64x64 patches centered at pixels.

nodes.name: Randomized actions
nodes.statement: To further explore augmentations, each patch of retinal images is composed of limited four randomized actions as follows: a) Flipping horizontally or vertically; b) Gamma correction of Saturation and Value (of the HSV colorspace) by raising pixels to a power in [0.25, 4]; c) Rotation by an angle in [-90, 90]; d) Scaling by a factor between 0.7 and 1.3.
nodes.statement_short: Apply up to four random transformations to each patch.

nodes.name: Structure prediction
nodes.statement: The structure prediction is mainly adopted in the testing by using the correlation between each pixel with its surrounding pixels of the retinal images. Like the patch-based average prediction method, different sliding window have different size and stride. Particularly, the edge pixels of the retinal images are predicted with less time due to the limitation.
nodes.statement_short: Test-time sliding-window prediction exploiting correlation of each pixel with its neighbours.

nodes.name: Structure prediction variants sp-1, sp-32, sp-64
nodes.statement: The windows of sp-1, sp-32 and sp-64 are the whole image, 32 $\times$ 32 and 64 $\times$ 64 respectively. The stride of sp-1, sp-32 and sp-64 are 1, 3 and 3 respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Window sizes (whole image, 32x32, 64x64) and strides (1,3,3) of the three variants.

nodes.name: Evaluation metrics
nodes.statement: {\bfseries Evaluation metrics} The evaluation metrics of our experiment is divided into two parts, one is in terms of area under ROC curve AUC, accuracy Acc, sensitivity Sens, specificity Spec and the other is the test speed that process one image (average time).

nodes.name: DRIVE AUC improvement
nodes.statement: In AUC, our method achieves 0.9826, which is 2.12\% higher than the state-of-the-art unsupervised method proposed by Azzopardi et al.and 0.36\% higher than the state-of-the-art supervised method proposed by Liskowski et al.

nodes.name: STARE AUC improvement
nodes.statement: Particularly, In AUC, our model achieves 0.9930, which is 4.33\% higher than Azzopardi's unsupervised approach and 0.02\% higher than Liskowski's supervised method.

nodes.name: CHASE AUC improvement
nodes.statement: In AUC, we achieves 98.65\%, which is higher than the best existing model proposed by Fraz et al who achieved 97.60\%.
conclusions: we achieves 98.65\%, which is higher than the best existing model proposed by Fraz et al who achieved 97.60\%

nodes.name: Structure prediction speeds up testing without accuracy loss
nodes.statement: These results of SP-1, SP-32 and SP-64 lead us to conclude that our model speeds up testing while ensuring high accuracy.
conclusions: our model speeds up testing while ensuring high accuracy

nodes.name: SP-1 test time
nodes.statement: In summary, the SP-1 achieves the test time of 3s, which is 7s faster than the state-of-the-art unsupervised method [6], and 87s faster than the state-of-the-art supervised method [12].
conclusions: the SP-1 achieves the test time of 3s

nodes.name: Robustness to lesions
nodes.statement: Compared with the real blood vessels, the probability value produced by our method is significantly lower for both bright and dark lesions and this shows the segmentation is less influenced by the presence of lesions.
conclusions: the segmentation is less influenced by the presence of lesions
